brief.situation: You are the security analyst at Halvard Logistics, a fictional freight company. Its internal assistant, AskOps, answers staff questions from the company's file libraries (retrieval-augmented generation). At 10:00 data loss prevention flags AskOps answering a contractor with salary figures and bank account numbers. Investigate, contain, keep evidence and report.
handover: Contractors get AskOps and an API key for their project. The source files carry sensitivity labels (Public, Internal, Confidential).
Permission-aware retrieval is a supported setting that was never turned on.
howItWorks: Each task takes analyst time: choose it, then let the work finish, which moves the clock by the minutes that task takes. The attacker keeps working on the same clock.
New alerts and log lines appear in the console as they happen.
When you declare the incident contained, you notify, write the record and explain your reasoning.

reviewLogs.label: Review the assistant's prompt and retrieval logs

effects.log: You read the prompt log and which document chunks each answer retrieved.

effects.finding: c-ventor has been asking systematically for salaries, bank details and HR files since 09:10, and three employees were shown HR chunks in answers to ordinary questions. No injection: the assistant is answering from data it should never have been able to reach for these users.

reviewConnector.label: Review the retrieval connector's permissions and index scope

effects.log: You check the indexer's service account, the libraries in the index and the retrieval settings.

effects.finding: The indexer runs as svc-askops-index with read access to every library, HR and Finance included. The files carry sensitivity labels, but the indexer ignores them, and retrieval does not check whether the asker can open a file. Least privilege and classification were lost at the integration.

writeup.question: For the incident record: why the assistant could leak this data, how you stopped it and why that holds, and who must be told.

parts.label: Cause
parts.criteria: Identifies the integration, not the model: a connector with read-all rights that ignored sensitivity labels, and retrieval that did not check the asker's permissions (sensitive information disclosure through vector and embedding weaknesses); no injection was needed.
parts.modelAnswer: The indexer read every library with one service account and ignored the labels, and retrieval never checked whether the asker could open a file, so anyone could get HR and Finance chunks by asking.

parts.label: Controls
parts.criteria: Disables the contractor and revokes the key; fixes retrieval with permission-aware access and labels or removes the sensitive collections (minimization); adds masking as a compensating control; explains why a system-prompt instruction is not access control.
parts.modelAnswer: I disabled c-ventor and the API key, switched retrieval to the asker's own permissions with labels honored, and turned on masking for bank and ID numbers. Telling the model not to reveal salaries changes nothing about what it retrieves.

parts.label: Scope and notice
parts.criteria: Preserves logs and an index manifest before deleting; lists every recipient of sensitive chunks; notifies privacy, legal, HR, AI governance and account owners.
parts.modelAnswer: I kept the prompt and retrieval logs and an index manifest, listed the four people who got sensitive chunks, and told privacy, legal, HR, AI governance and the account owners.

expertPath.text: Bring in privacy; read the prompt and retrieval logs: systematic questions, and employees shown HR data too.
Disable the contractor and the API key; preserve the logs and an index manifest.

contained.headline: Good: fixed where the data lives
contained.body: The model only says what retrieval hands it. You fixed the integration's access and kept the assistant running.

containedGaps.headline: Contained, with gaps
containedGaps.body: The leak is stopped. The criteria show what cost you: the assistant switched off, contracts pulled first, or time.

bulkLeak.headline: Walked by a script
bulkLeak.body: A system-prompt line, or leaving the contractor's key live, let a script ask its way through every folder the connector could read.

evidenceLost.headline: Index deleted first
evidenceLost.body: Without the logs and a manifest, privacy cannot say whose records went to whom. Keep them, then delete.

stillLeaking.headline: Closed too soon
stillLeaking.body: Disabling one user leaves everyone else able to retrieve the same data; a prompt line is not access control (LLM02, LLM08).

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: The model leaked what retrieval gave it: a connector with read-all rights that ignored sensitivity labels, and retrieval that never checked the asker's permissions. Disable the contractor and revoke the API key, preserve the prompt and retrieval logs and an index manifest, switch retrieval to the asker's own permissions with labels honored (or remove the sensitive collections), add masking at the gateway, list every recipient, and notify privacy, legal, HR, AI governance and the account owners. A system-prompt instruction is not access control.
